# Evaluated Applications: products, tools and evidence in full

Data that answers in microseconds and language models that run in a browser tab. .NET libraries you add with one command, and tools to try now.

Updated: 2026-10-15

## Products

### Phasor: do a thousand things in one pass

Build stores that answer exactly, replicas that sync by their differences and tables that repair themselves. One pass applies a thousand operators.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/phasor/
- Package EvaluatedApplications.Phasor, release 2.17.0: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.Phasor`
- Used by: HoloDb, AlgFormer, HoloVoxel

Do a thousand things in one pass.

Build stores that answer exactly, replicas that sync by sending only what differs, and tables that repair themselves. Every item and every operator lives in one array, so one sweep moves all of it.

- 0.17 to 0.44 ms: for one pass that applies from 1 to 10,368 operators at once
- 200 of 200: trials recovering 64 stored items exactly, where a float baseline held 4 at the same storage
- 12,800 of 12,800: reads past capacity answered with a clear no. It never guesses
- 0.6 ms: to read a whole 3,150-slot page, exactly

The numbers:
- One pass, from 1 to 10,368 operators. Apply took 0.17 to 0.44 ms per call over two runs, with no trend in the number of elements. Building the same store from the moved items took 3 ms at 1 element and 1,916 ms at 1,000. Conditions: a 10,464-cell store (GF(13,879), 6 flag bits, S_3, time period 27, joint flags by order by time, key capacity 4, a continuous component, 10 items on four keys), random kernels, the mean of 20 calls after one warm-up, Release build, a loaded i9-11950H.
- 64 items recovered exactly. At equal storage (about 2,000 to 2,600 bits), the exact key view recovered 64 items in 200 of 200 trials. The best float baseline reached 95 percent at 4 items. That is 16 times the items at these budgets. The benchmark is not part of the shipped package.
- A clear no past capacity. Past capacity (65 to 96 items), the keys-only hologram refused 12,800 of 12,800 trials with no wrong answer. Every float baseline answered wrongly every time.
- A whole page in 0.6 ms. With a complete key band, reading a 3,150-slot page costs about 0.6 ms (188 to 246 ns per slot). Building a page from a count vector is about 100 times faster than adding its keys one by one.

What you can build:
- Database answers in a millisecond. Read a whole 3,150-slot page of exact counts in about 0.6 ms. HoloDb serves COUNT, SUM, GROUP BY and joins from slices of a store like this.
- Replicas that sync by their differences. Send one small message sized to what differs, not to your data. Ten thousand shared items and one different on each side take 192 bytes, and the other side reads the exact difference.
- A store that repairs itself. Lose up to five values and get them back, 300 of 300 times. Catch one corrupted cell in either copy, 10,000 of 10,000 times. Rebuild a lost store from its group, 100 of 100 times.
- A memory that reads exactly. Store pairs and read them back without drift. At equal storage, recall held at 100 percent from 2 to 32 pairs, where a float bundle fell to 21.9 percent at 32.
- Age and reshape everything at once. Age, relabel, diffuse or bind every item in one pass. The cost follows the size of the store, not the number of items in it.
- Any question, one read. Count the items that match any condition on their flags, however tangled, in one read. Ask for counts, shares and parity from one query.

Quick start:

```csharp
using Phasor;

var shape = new HologramShape { KeyCapacity = 4, FlagBits = 3, TimePeriod = 7, JointFaces = HologramFaces.Flags | HologramFaces.Time };
var store = new Pleroma(shape);                          // 96 cells for this shape, whatever the item count
store.Add(new HologramItem(Key: 10, Flags: 0b001, Time: 0), 3);
store.Add(new HologramItem(Key: 20, Flags: 0b010, Time: 2), 2);
store.Add(new HologramItem(Key: 30, Flags: 0b100, Time: 4), 1);

if (store.TryItems(out var items))
    foreach (var (item, count) in items)
        Console.WriteLine($"key {item.Key} flags {item.Flags} time {item.Time} count {count}");

var kernel = new PleromaKernel(shape);
kernel.Add(weight: 1L);                                  // keep every item
kernel.Add(flagMask: 0b001, timeShift: 1, weight: 2L);   // and twice: flip bit 0, age one tick
store.Apply(kernel);                                     // one pass over all 96 cells

if (store.TryKeys(out var keys))
    foreach (var k in keys)
        Console.WriteLine($"key total {k}");
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" ", store.Flags()));
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" ", store.Times()));
```

Output:

```text
key 10 flags 1 time 0 count 3
key 20 flags 2 time 2 count 2
key 30 flags 4 time 4 count 1
key total (10, 9)
key total (20, 6)
key total (30, 3)
6 3 2 4 1 2 0 0
3 6 2 4 1 2 0
```

7 of 36 operators that transform the store join one kernel: a weighted sum of them applies to every stored item in one shared pass. All 45 reads answer from the store array in one pass each (CausalReads is the stated exception: one pass per prefix). This is a fact about reads, not part of the score.

11 established ideas, one store. The Pleroma is a new construction. It is one store that satisfies every brick in the table below. Each brick is established work and is credited in its row. Each row gives what the brick offers on its own, the operation of the Pleroma that carries it, and the check that the operation passes.
- Reed-Solomon and BCH syndrome decoding (Reed and Solomon 1960; Bose and Ray-Chaudhuri 1960): Recovers up to K distinct symbols exactly from 2K+1 power sums, and refuses beyond that. In the Pleroma: The key view: `TryKeys` and `TryItems` read the key line by syndrome decoding and refuse past `KeyCapacity`. Proof: Keys exact in 30 of 30 trials at 16 keys, and refused in 30 of 30 trials at 17 and 20 keys.
- Berlekamp-Massey (Berlekamp 1968; Massey 1969): Finds the shortest recurrence that generates a syndrome sequence. In the Pleroma: The decoder of the key view (`CycleDecoder`), with a re-encode check on every decode. CycleHologram uses the same decoder. Proof: CycleHologram decodes exactly across the capacity sweeps; the Pleroma key view and CycleHologram agree on one decoder.
- PinSketch and minisketch set reconciliation (Talbot et al. 2012; Poinsot et al. 2017): A sketch sized to the difference of two sets decodes that difference. In the Pleroma: Replica reconciliation: two holograms subtract exactly and the signed difference decodes. The Pleroma subtracts exactly, and its key view decodes the difference up to `KeyCapacity`. Proof: CycleHologram decodes the exact signed multiset difference across the tested cases; Pleroma `Subtract` is exact across a sequence of merge, tick, relabel and serialize steps.
- Walsh-Hadamard transform (Fourier analysis on Z_2^m): The spectrum of a Boolean function on flag words, from which the count under any predicate is one inner product. In the Pleroma: `CountWhere`, `CountWhereByTime` and `CountWhereByArrangement` count the items under any predicate of the flag word in one read; `Attend` uses the same contraction. Proof: Predicate counts equal direct counting in 1,515 of 1,515 cases on three fields.
- Group convolution (Fourier analysis on finite groups): The product of two group-algebra elements is a convolution, and in the Fourier domain it is a product on each block. In the Pleroma: `Bind` (keys add, flags XOR, arrangements compose, ticks add, counts multiply) and kernel `Apply` (a product on each block of stored harmonics). Proof: `Bind` equals the store of all pairs, cell for cell and view for view, in 35 of 35 cases across five shapes. `Apply` equals the store of moved items, cell for cell, for kernels of 1, 10, 100 and 1,000 elements and for the whole group.
- Chinese remainder theorem (classical): Joins residues modulo coprime moduli into one residue modulo their product. In the Pleroma: `CombineCycles` joins two coprime complete key cycles into one key space. Each pair of keys becomes the key with both residues. Proof: `CombineCycles` equals the store of Chinese-remainder pairs in 12 of 12 cases on two fields.
- Hamming codes and their syndromes (Hamming 1950): The syndrome of a word locates a single error. In the Pleroma: `Syndrome` counts the stored words per Hamming syndrome, for 3, 7 or 15 flag bits. Proof: All 112 single errors of Hamming(7,4) are located, and all 336 double errors are sent to a wrong third position.
- Galois linear feedback shift registers: A linear recurrence over GF(2) with a period set by its polynomial. In the Pleroma: `ShiftRegister` steps every stored flag word through the register, for any number of steps in one pass. Proof: The stepped store equals the store of stepped words. The recorded periods are 255 and 63 for primitive polynomials.
- Frobenius map on GF(2^m) (finite field arithmetic): Squaring in a binary field is a linear map on its elements. In the Pleroma: `Frobenius` squares every stored flag word modulo a polynomial, for any number of steps in one pass. Proof: The store equals the store of squared words. Its order on GF(2^8) is exactly 8.
- Time diffusion on a cycle (Markov chains): A walk that stays with some probability and otherwise moves one step. In the Pleroma: `Diffuse` runs the walk on every item at once and gives exact expected counts, scaled by `TimeScale`. `Tick` ages every item exactly. Proof: Expected counts are exact over 20 steps on two fields, and the recorded run is exact over 600 steps.
- Holographic Reduced Representations: binding and bundling (Plate 1995): Key-value pairs superposed by a sum and read back by correlation. The read is approximate, and its noise grows with load. In the Pleroma: The continuous component is the bundle. `Density`, `Similarity` and `FadedTimes` read it with graded similarity. The exact cells are read by decoding. Proof: The continuous bundle is a slice of the store, and its similarity is the kernel of the component (`PleromaContinuousTests`, CF1).

Its structure follows three families of symmetry, taken in a fixed order: the cyclic key group, the flag cube Z_2^m and the symmetric group S_k. The time cycle is a cyclic family of the same kind. The eight rungs run in that order, and each one adds operations to those before it. Every operation is checked against a brute-force rebuild of the same answer.

Put it to work:
- HoloDb aggregate plane. Database.EnablePleroma(table, options) derives a Pleroma from a table's columns and serves COUNT, SUM, GROUP BY, WHERE, COUNT DISTINCT, MIN and MAX of dimensions, HAVING, and a single equi-join COUNT or SUM from exact slices. It holds in-RAM tables and is not persisted, so call it again after Open. AVG and other shapes use the engine.
- Page store, larger than memory. Pages of one shape are stored as records with a check prime that verifies every record, parity groups that rebuild one lost record each, restore points, and journal numbers so replay applies each add once. It needs a complete key band, and a reader may see a batch half applied while it runs.
- Replica reconciliation. Two replicas each hold a CycleHologram. The one with the difference sends its hologram, and the other subtracts its own and decodes the exact signed difference. The message is sized to the difference, not to the data. It decodes when the difference has at most the capacity's worth of distinct symbols, so size the capacity to the largest difference you expect.
- Batch relabel, age and diffuse. Tick, Diffuse, RelabelFlags, RelabelArrangements, ShiftKeys, ScaleKeys (on a complete key band) and Apply(kernel) each act on every stored item at once. A mix of different harmonic permutations costs one pass per term. Diffuse readbacks need TimeScale times the total to stay within half the field.

When another tool fits better:
- A single item, or a few keys. Each Add touches every cell of the store. A dictionary is cheaper for one lookup, and the sparse page (PleromaSparsePage) suits a few keys.
- Floating-point similarity at high dimension. The Pleroma is exact and has no key-addressed similarity. For graded similarity use the continuous component (ContinuousFade) or the HoloCodec similarity search.
- More distinct keys than the capacity, without a bigger shape. The key view refuses past KeyCapacity. Raising it costs 2K+1 numbers per key line.
- Choices. argmax, softmax and sampling are not linear, so they are read-time steps (Attend's shares, Sample), not kernel elements.
- Counts past the field's range. Weighted kernels on a small field need headroom. On a large field the limit is about 1.15 x 10^18 per count.

Know before you start:
- The key view is exact recovery of a multiset of keys, not similarity search. There is no key-addressed attention.
- Counts are exact within the field's signed range. No read detects a wrap past that range.
- The Pleroma runs on the CPU. There is no GPU kernel.
- Exact arithmetic is not faster in general. A Pleroma read costs one or more transforms, and a float bundle read is one correlation. The Pleroma gives you exactness and many views on one array.
- A kernel is refused on a store with a check prime.
- Locating the contradiction on a relation face is not provided.

#### Phasor docs (https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/phasor/docs/)

Task-oriented notes with complete programs. Each example was compiled and run against the published package, and the output shown is what it printed.

##### Reading a Pleroma

A store is built item by item with Add, which takes a signed count, and Remove erases one copy. The key view keeps exactly the items with distinct keys up to KeyCapacity and refuses past that. Every other view reads its own slice of the array and stays exact at any load, within the field's range.

TryKeys returns the key, total count and the flag word, arrangement or tick when there is one per key. TryItems returns whole items when each key has one value per face factor. Both return false past capacity, never a wrong answer.

- Flags, Near, Nearest: Flags returns the exact count at every flag word. Near(x, r) counts items whose flags differ from x in at most r bits, and Nearest(x) returns the nearest stored words with their distances.
- Arrangements, SignBalance: Counts per arrangement of up to 5 things, and the even-minus-odd balance.
- Times, Tick, Diffuse: Counts per tick. Tick ages every item, and Diffuse runs a lazy random walk over time on every item at once. Time views then return TimeScale times the exact expected counts.
- JointCounts: Set JointFaces, for example Flags and Time, and JointCounts returns the exact joint counts. The joint slice holds the product of the faces' sizes, so size it deliberately.
- CountWhere, Compile: Count the items whose flag word satisfies any predicate with one inner product. Compile prepares a predicate for repeated queries, and CountWhereByTime and CountWhereByArrangement give the count per tick or per arrangement.
- BitCounts, FlagParity, TryFindConflicts: Per-bit counts and the XOR of every stored word from a few cells, and the keys that carry more than one flag word or arrangement.

##### Bind two stores

store.Bind(other) binds every pair of items at once: keys add, flag words XOR, arrangements compose, ticks add, and counts multiply. The cost is one product per order representation, not per pair of items. Binding with a one-item store shifts the whole store on every face together, and binding with a larger store applies the mix of all those shifts.

```csharp
using Phasor;

var shape = new HologramShape { KeyCapacity = 8, FlagBits = 4, TimePeriod = 9 };
var store = new Pleroma(shape);
store.Add(new HologramItem(Key: 10, Flags: 0b0011, Time: 2), 3);
store.Add(new HologramItem(Key: 20, Flags: 0b0111, Time: 5), 1);

// Bind with a one-item store: every item moves by the same key, flags and time shift.
var shift = new Pleroma(shape);
shift.Add(new HologramItem(Key: 1, Flags: 0b0001, Time: 1));
store.Bind(shift);

if (store.TryItems(out var items))
    foreach (var (item, count) in items)
        Console.WriteLine($"{item.Key}: flags {item.Flags}, time {item.Time}, count {count}");
```

Output:

```text
11: flags 2, time 3, count 3
21: flags 6, time 6, count 1
```

##### Apply a weighted kernel in one pass

A PleromaKernel is a weighted sum of any number of flag flips, arrangement relabellings and time shifts, held as one harmonic factor per stored harmonic. store.Apply(kernel) gives exactly the store you would get by moving every item by every element and adding the copies, at a cost that does not depend on how many elements the kernel holds. Kernels add and compose, and Diffuse is the two-element case.

The example applies one identity plus two copies of an item that has a flag flipped and a tick added, to three items. Every flag and time count changes at once.

```csharp
using Phasor;

var store = new Pleroma(new HologramShape
{
    KeyCapacity = 4,
    FlagBits = 3,
    TimePeriod = 7,
    JointFaces = HologramFaces.Flags | HologramFaces.Time,
});
store.Add(new HologramItem(Key: 10, Flags: 0b001, Time: 0), 3);
store.Add(new HologramItem(Key: 20, Flags: 0b010, Time: 2), 2);
store.Add(new HologramItem(Key: 30, Flags: 0b100, Time: 4), 1);
Console.WriteLine("before flags " + string.Join(" ", store.Flags()));
Console.WriteLine("before times " + string.Join(" ", store.Times()));

// One kernel: 1x identity plus 2x (flip flag bit 0 and age one tick), applied to every item in one pass.
var kernel = new PleromaKernel(store.Shape);
kernel.Add(weight: 1L);
kernel.Add(flagMask: 0b001, timeShift: 1, weight: 2L);
store.Apply(kernel);

Console.WriteLine("after flags  " + string.Join(" ", store.Flags()));
Console.WriteLine("after times  " + string.Join(" ", store.Times()));
```

Output:

```text
before flags 0 3 2 0 1 0 0 0
before times 3 0 2 0 1 0 0
after flags  6 3 2 4 1 2 0 0
after times  3 6 2 4 1 2 0
```

##### Bit counts and parity

BitCounts gives the exact count of items with each bit set, and FlagParity gives the XOR of every stored word, both from a handful of cells.

```csharp
using Phasor;

var store = new Pleroma(new HologramShape { FlagBits = 4, KeyCapacity = 8 });
store.Add(new HologramItem(Key: 1, Flags: 0b0011), 2);   // two copies
store.Add(new HologramItem(Key: 1, Flags: 0b0110), 1);   // one copy
store.Add(new HologramItem(Key: 2, Flags: 0b0001), 3);   // three copies

long[] bitCounts = store.BitCounts();                     // exact count of items with each bit set
uint parity = store.FlagParity();                         // XOR of every stored word
Console.WriteLine($"{bitCounts[0]} {bitCounts[1]} {bitCounts[2]} {bitCounts[3]} parity {parity}");
```

Output:

```text
5 3 1 0 parity 7
```

##### More operations

- ScaleKeys, CombineCycles: With CompleteKeys a store keeps every harmonic of a small key cycle. ScaleKeys(u) relabels every key a to u a in place, and CombineCycles joins two stores on coprime cycles into one on their product, by the Chinese remainder theorem.
- Frobenius, ShiftRegister: On a store built without per-bit item lines, Frobenius squares every flag word in GF(2^m) and ShiftRegister steps every word through a linear shift register, exactly, any number of steps in one pass.
- Syndrome, IsIndependent, Sample: Count stored words per Hamming syndrome, test in exact integers whether joint counts are the product of their marginals, and draw one value of any view with probability count over total.
- RelationFace, ChargeLattice: Store relations between a small set of keys and read a loop's winding, its frustration parity and the direction of its net circulation. Integer offsets on a periodic lattice give each cube an exact charge.
- Eliminate: With one flag bit as a label, every stored word is an example, and Eliminate solves for the parity rule over GF(2) that fits every example, or reports that none does.
- Dense pages: With CompleteKeys a store is a page of up to 4,096 slots in which every slot reads back exactly. FromCounts and AddCounts build a page from a count vector in one transform, CountWhereKey sums any function of the key in one read, and InnerProduct gives the exact equi-join sum of two pages.
- Sparse pages: PleromaSparsePage keeps exact counts over keys anywhere in a huge key set in memory proportional to the keys present, with exact merges and draws.
- Redundancy: ReservedKeys with Verify and Repair detect and rebuild lost harmonics, CheckPrime and VerifyCheck detect corruption of either copy, and PleromaParity rebuilds any one lost store of a group.
- SQL-style compositions: Restrict, Support (and so COUNT DISTINCT), MapCounts, sums per group and joins are exact, built from the operations above.

##### CycleHologram: the keys-only case

CycleHologram is the Pleroma with keys only, kept as its own type. The phasor bundle, a sum of phasors, is a hologram: many items superposed in one fixed-size vector, read out approximately, with crosstalk that grows with load. CycleHologram is the same superposition on the discrete cycle of a finite field. Each symbol is an element of the cycle, the hologram holds power sums of the stored elements, and the readout is algebraic instead of statistical, so there is no similarity threshold and no rounding.

A hologram of capacity k holds 2k+1 eight-byte elements, and TryDecode returns every stored symbol with its signed count when at most k distinct symbols are stored. With k+1 distinct symbols decode always refuses. Every decode is re-encoded and must reproduce every stored element. Holograms add as a multiset union, subtract as an exact signed difference, and serialize with their field metadata.

Each replica in the second example holds 10,000 items and the hologram has capacity 4, so it finds what differs by exchanging one small hologram sized to the difference, not to the data. If the replicas differ in more than the capacity, TryDecode returns false, so size the capacity to the largest difference you expect.

The decoder is the syndrome decoder of Reed-Solomon and BCH codes (Berlekamp-Massey), the construction behind the PinSketch set sketch and the minisketch library.

```csharp
using Phasor;

var stock = new CycleHologram(capacity: 8);
stock.Add(CycleHologram.Symbol("apples"), 10);
stock.Add(42, 5);                                   // integer symbols are exact
stock.Add(CycleHologram.Symbol("oranges"), 3);

if (stock.TryDecode(out var items))
{
    foreach (var (symbol, count) in items.OrderBy(i => i.Item2))
        Console.WriteLine($"count {count}");        // every count is exact
}
```

Output:

```text
count 3
count 5
count 10
```

```csharp
using Phasor;

var a = new CycleHologram(capacity: 4);
var b = new CycleHologram(capacity: 4);
for (ulong id = 0; id < 10_000; id++) { a.Add(id); b.Add(id); }
a.Add(777_001);        // only on A
b.Add(777_002, 2);     // only on B, two copies

byte[] wire = a.Serialize();                   // what A sends
Console.WriteLine($"wire size {wire.Length} bytes");
var delta = CycleHologram.Deserialize(wire);
delta.Subtract(b);                             // B subtracts its own hologram: A minus B
if (delta.TryDecode(out var diff))
    foreach (var (symbol, count) in diff.OrderBy(d => d.Item1))
        Console.WriteLine($"{symbol}: {count}");
```

Output:

```text
wire size 192 bytes
777001: 1
777002: -2
```

##### The phasor codecs

Phasor gives you two operations. Encode turns a number into a face with its value as phase, and gives a symbol a salted hash-based random signature. Compose with bind (complex multiply per component) to build relationships, bundle (sum) to collect sets, and unbind (conjugate) to extract parts, and read out with correlation. On the linear band of a face, bind is addition. On the log band it is multiplication. There is no separate calculator: arithmetic is the composition.

PhasorCodec has a fixed width of 256 reals, with a frozen identity prefix and a learned orbital tail, and is built for neural models. HoloCodec has a configurable width, uses SIMD, has a planar layout and a memoized number cache, and is built for holographic storage and similarity search at scale. Do not mix faces between the two.

```csharp
using Phasor;

// Encode a number and some symbols
double[] five = PhasorCodec.Encode("5");
double[] three = PhasorCodec.Encode("3");
double[] age = PhasorCodec.Encode("age");
double[] name = PhasorCodec.Encode("name");
double[] hello = PhasorCodec.Encode("hello");

// Bind two numbers: adds them on the linear band
double[] fivePlusThree = PhasorCodec.Bind(five, three);
Console.WriteLine($"5 + 3 = {PhasorCodec.DecodeSum(fivePlusThree, max: 10)}");

// Bind each value to a role, bundle the pairs into one record, then unbind a role to read its value back
double[] record = PhasorCodec.Bundle(PhasorCodec.Bind(age, five), PhasorCodec.Bind(name, hello));
double[] ageField = PhasorCodec.Unbind(record, age);
Console.WriteLine($"age field matches 5 better than 3: {PhasorCodec.Correlate(ageField, five) > PhasorCodec.Correlate(ageField, three)}");

// For larger workloads and similarity search, HoloCodec is SIMD and configurable in width
var codec = new HoloCodec(dim: 1024);
double[] encoded = codec.Encode("hello");
Console.WriteLine($"HoloCodec self-similarity is positive: {HoloCodec.Dot(encoded, codec.Encode("hello")) > 0}");
```

Output:

```text
5 + 3 = 8
age field matches 5 better than 3: True
HoloCodec self-similarity is positive: True
```

##### Hologram: readable algebra with operators

Hologram wraps a phasor face with operators for readability and prototyping. It is a readonly struct around a double array, so it converts freely to and from arrays without copying.

Bind is the operator *, per-component complex multiply. Bundle is +, a component-wise sum that merges holograms into one superposition. Unbind is /, multiplying by the conjugate. Correlate is a method that gives a dot product, and ~ flips the sign of the imaginary parts. Readout by correlation is approximate. For an exact readout use Pleroma, or CycleHologram for keys only.

Read those four numbers carefully, because the two fields behave differently. The name field separates completely: 128.59 for the right value against -1.96 for the wrong one. Two symbols get independent random signatures, so an unrelated symbol correlates at the noise floor, near zero.

The age field separates by less than 3x: 32.59 for 7 against 13.39 for 5. That is the codec telling the truth. A number is encoded as a phase proportional to its value, so 5 and 7 are similar faces and 5 and 500 are not. Numbers carry a metric and symbols do not. If you want numbers to behave like symbols, encode them with FromSymbol instead of FromNumber, and give up arithmetic to get it.

So correlation separates signal from noise for symbols, and separates signal from nearby signal only by distance for numbers. Design the readout accordingly: take an argmax over candidate values rather than a threshold, which is what DecodeSum and DecodeProduct do.

```csharp
using Phasor;

var dim = 256;  // Hologram default dimension

// A record is a superposition of role-value pairs
var nameRole = Hologram.FromSymbol("name", dim);
var lily = Hologram.FromSymbol("Lily", dim);
var ageRole = Hologram.FromSymbol("age", dim);
var seven = Hologram.FromNumber(7, dim);
var record = Hologram.Zero(dim) + nameRole * lily + ageRole * seven;   // bind, then bundle

// Unbind a role and correlate with candidate values
var nameField = record / nameRole;
var ageField = record / ageRole;
Console.WriteLine($"Name field has Lily:  {nameField.Correlate(lily):F2}");
Console.WriteLine($"Name field has John:  {nameField.Correlate(Hologram.FromSymbol("John", dim)):F2}");
Console.WriteLine($"Age field has 7:  {ageField.Correlate(seven):F2}");
Console.WriteLine($"Age field has 5:  {ageField.Correlate(Hologram.FromNumber(5, dim)):F2}");
```

Output:

```text
Name field has Lily:  128.59
Name field has John:  -1.96
Age field has 7:  32.59
Age field has 5:  13.39
```

##### Arithmetic with numbers

When you bind two numbers their bands compose. The face carries both operations at once, and you read out the band you care about. Arithmetic is composition, not calculation.

The operators allocate a new array per operation. In tight loops or accumulation, use the in-place static methods BindInto, BundleInto and UnbindInto with a buffer you allocate once. At typical dimensions the allocating Bind operator is about 1.7 times slower than BindInto.

```csharp
using Phasor;

var dim = 256;

// Linear band: binding two numbers adds them
var sumEncoded = Hologram.FromNumber(3, dim) * Hologram.FromNumber(5, dim);
Console.WriteLine(PhasorCodec.DecodeSum(sumEncoded, max: 20));

// Log band: binding two numbers multiplies them
var productEncoded = Hologram.FromNumber(2, dim) * Hologram.FromNumber(4, dim);
Console.WriteLine(PhasorCodec.DecodeProduct(productEncoded, max: 16));

// In a loop, use the in-place methods: they reuse one buffer instead of allocating per call
double[] accumulator = new double[dim];
for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++)
    Hologram.BundleInto(accumulator, Hologram.FromNumber(i, dim).Reals);
Console.WriteLine($"accumulated {accumulator.Length} components");
```

Output:

```text
8
8
accumulated 256 components
```

##### Things to know

- Layouts do not mix: Hologram uses the interleaved layout, the same as PhasorCodec. HoloCodec is planar, with all reals then all imaginary parts, and produces garbage if given an interleaved face.
- Dimension floor: PhasorCodec requires an even dimension of at least 128: 64 frozen reals and at least 64 orbital. Odd dimensions align down, and anything below 128 throws an ArgumentException.
- .Reals is live: The Reals property returns the internal array, not a copy, so changing it changes the hologram. Use it read-only or pass it to the in-place methods.
- Small fields wrap: Every view's count must lie within half the field per prime. On a small test field, large kernel weights wrap, so compare cells there instead of counts.

#### The Pleroma: one array, every question (https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/phasor/pleroma/)

One array of exact integers holds your items. Ask it for counts by key, by flag word, by Hamming distance, by arrangement and by time. Apply a thousand operators in one pass.

##### What it is

The Pleroma is a fixed-size array of exact integers (finite-field arithmetic) that holds a multiset of items. Each item is a key, optionally with a flag word, an arrangement and a tick. One array answers many questions: counts by key, by flag word, by Hamming distance, by arrangement, by tick, and joint counts over any chosen faces.

The store holds a harmonic transform on the product of the key cycle, the flag cube, the symmetric group and the time cycle. Each component of the transform is a harmonic. The store keeps only the harmonics its views need, and each view reads its own slice of the array.

##### The three faces

A Pleroma view is one of three faces of the same array.

- Syzygy (the key cycle, and the time cycle for tick views): Key-addressed lookup: counts per key, whole items with signed counts, and the relation face. Key views refuse past KeyCapacity distinct keys, returning false rather than a wrong answer.
- Monad (the arrangements, S_k, 2 to 5 things): Counts per arrangement, even minus odd, tick maps, and the composition and conjugation of arrangements.
- Ouroboros (the flag cube, up to 16 bits): Counts per flag word, Hamming retrieval, Boolean predicates through the Walsh spectrum, bit maps and parity.

##### The pyramid

The operations form a grid of 8 rungs by 3 faces, plus one read-time operation (the lid): 25 cells in all. Every cell is a public member of Pleroma, checked against a brute-force or naive rebuild of the same answer, and every whole-store operation applies to all items in one pass.

Turn the pyramid, select a cell, or colour it by kind. Each cell shows its API and what it was checked against.

##### The rungs as a ladder

Read down the table: each rung adds one thing a single pass can do, and names what it superposes and the operator that does it.

##### One store, many items

One Pleroma holds many items at once. Every whole-store operation applies to all of them in a single pass, and the cost of that pass does not depend on the number of items stored. A mix of different harmonic permutations (key scaling, bit maps and conjugation, rung 5) costs one pass per term.

The example holds three items with key capacity 4, then applies one kernel of 1x identity plus 2x (flip flag bit 0, age 1 tick). Press Replay to watch the pass move through the store, or switch between the counts before and after.

The kernel applies exactly the store you would get by moving every item by every element and adding the copies. The measured cost of the pass is on the evidence page, beside the cost of doing it item by item.

```csharp
using Phasor;

var store = new Pleroma(new HologramShape
{
    KeyCapacity = 4,
    FlagBits = 3,
    TimePeriod = 7,
    JointFaces = HologramFaces.Flags | HologramFaces.Time,
});
store.Add(new HologramItem(Key: 10, Flags: 0b001, Time: 0), 3);
store.Add(new HologramItem(Key: 20, Flags: 0b010, Time: 2), 2);
store.Add(new HologramItem(Key: 30, Flags: 0b100, Time: 4), 1);
Console.WriteLine("before flags " + string.Join(" ", store.Flags()));
Console.WriteLine("before times " + string.Join(" ", store.Times()));

// One kernel: 1x identity plus 2x (flip flag bit 0 and age one tick), applied to every item in one pass.
var kernel = new PleromaKernel(store.Shape);
kernel.Add(weight: 1L);
kernel.Add(flagMask: 0b001, timeShift: 1, weight: 2L);
store.Apply(kernel);

Console.WriteLine("after flags  " + string.Join(" ", store.Flags()));
Console.WriteLine("after times  " + string.Join(" ", store.Times()));
```

Output:

```text
before flags 0 3 2 0 1 0 0 0
before times 3 0 2 0 1 0 0
after flags  6 3 2 4 1 2 0 0
after times  3 6 2 4 1 2 0
```

##### The capacity rule: 2K+1, and the refusal

A Pleroma with key capacity K stores exactly 2K+1 harmonics per key line. Any store of K or fewer keys is decoded exactly, by Berlekamp-Massey syndrome decoding as in Reed-Solomon codes. All K items are held at once in one 2K+1 entry array, and reading any face (flags, arrangements, times) gives exact counts for all of them.

Past capacity, decoding fails at K+1 keys and returns false instead of guessing, so the store never returns a wrong answer. Add keys below to see what the package returned for each number of distinct keys.

##### Bind and Attend

store.Bind(other) binds every pair of items from two stores in one pass: keys add (mod the key space), flags XOR, arrangements compose, ticks add and counts multiply. The cost is one matrix product per order representation, not per pair of items.

Attend(query, face) reads three things from one contraction of the store for a flag predicate (an exact match, a partial match on a mask, or any Boolean function). Counts per value are the exact counts at each matched flag word, arrangement or tick. Shares are those counts divided by the total, summing to 1. Parity is the sign of the total. The cost is one spectrum and one inner product, whatever the number of items.

```csharp
using Phasor;

var shape = new HologramShape { KeyCapacity = 8, FlagBits = 4, TimePeriod = 9 };
var store = new Pleroma(shape);
store.Add(new HologramItem(Key: 10, Flags: 0b0011, Time: 2), 3);
store.Add(new HologramItem(Key: 20, Flags: 0b0111, Time: 5), 1);

// Bind with a one-item store: every item moves by the same key, flags and time shift.
var shift = new Pleroma(shape);
shift.Add(new HologramItem(Key: 1, Flags: 0b0001, Time: 1));
store.Bind(shift);

if (store.TryItems(out var items))
    foreach (var (item, count) in items)
        Console.WriteLine($"{item.Key}: flags {item.Flags}, time {item.Time}, count {count}");
```

Output:

```text
11: flags 2, time 3, count 3
21: flags 6, time 6, count 1
```

##### Keys, bit maps and exact checks

- Shift, scale and combine keys: ShiftKeys(k) adds k to every key in place. ScaleKeys(u) multiplies every key by a unit, or gathers several keys to one for a non-unit. CombineCycles(a, b) joins two stores on coprime key cycles by the Chinese remainder theorem. Scaling and combining need the optional CompleteKeys configuration.
- Frobenius and shift registers: Frobenius(modulus, steps) squares every flag word as a polynomial over GF(2), and ShiftRegister(polynomial, steps) steps every word through a linear shift register, each exactly and in one pass.
- Exact repair and redundancy: ReservedKeys lets Verify detect and Repair rebuild up to r lost or corrupted key-line harmonics. CheckPrime mirrors every cell in a second prime so VerifyCheck detects any corruption of one copy. PleromaParity keeps the exact sum of a group of stores and rebuilds any one lost store.
- Dense and sparse pages: With CompleteKeys, a store is a dense page of up to 4,096 slots where Count and Counts read every slot exactly in one transform. PleromaSparsePage holds exact counts over keys anywhere in a huge key set in memory proportional to the keys present.

##### Built on the Pleroma

The HoloDb holographic plane uses the Pleroma as its data store. COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX, GROUP BY, HAVING, COUNT DISTINCT, WHERE, JOIN and any Boolean predicate are exact on it.

##### Limits

- Keys: The key view is exact recovery of a multiset of keys, not similarity search. Capacity K keeps 2K+1 harmonics per key line and decodes up to K distinct keys.
- Range: Counts are exact within the field's signed range, about 1.15 x 10^18 on the default field. No read detects a wrap past that range.
- Kernels: A kernel is refused on a store with a check prime.
- Hardware: The Pleroma runs on the CPU. There is no GPU kernel.
- Speed: Exact arithmetic is not faster than a float bundle for a single read. The Pleroma gives you exactness and many views on one array.
- Relations: Locating the contradiction on a relation face is not provided.

##### Prior art

- Reed-Solomon and BCH codes: Syndrome decoding (Reed and Solomon 1960, Berlekamp 1968, Massey 1969).
- Berlekamp-Massey: The algorithm for finding minimal polynomials that the key decode uses.
- PinSketch and minisketch: Set sketches built on the same construction (Talbot and others 2012, Poinsot and others 2017).
- Holographic reduced representations: Plate's 1995 representation, the approximate store the Pleroma is compared with.
- Fourier analysis on finite groups: Fourier analysis on finite groups and Krawtchouk polynomials underlie the views.

Licence: Commercial licence for commercial use. Evaluation and non-commercial use are permitted. Terms at https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/licence/

### EvalApp: a self-tuning async pipeline runtime for .NET

Run everything at once without overloading anything. Gates on every resource, sagas that undo failures, and a tuner that finds the right speed.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/evalapp/
- Package EvaluatedApplications.EvalApp, release 4.4.1: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.EvalApp`
- Package EvaluatedApplications.EvalApp.Neural, release 2.0.3: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.EvalApp.Neural`
- Used by: HoloDb, AlgFormer, Prose, Tracer

Run it all at once without overloading anything.

Describe a process as plain steps. EvalApp gates every database, disk and network call at a bound you set, undoes failed work in reverse order, and can tune the bound for you. No broker, no services to stand up.

- 7 of 7: recorded runs where the most downloads in flight equalled the gate bound
- 1,113 ms to 139 ms: time to finish 24 jobs at a bound of 1 and at the best bound, 8
- 2.9 times: slower with all 24 jobs running at once than at the best bound

EvalApp replaces the plumbing that every real async .NET codebase ends up writing by hand: a SemaphoreSlim to stop a flood of requests hammering a database, a guessed constant for how many things run at once, a Task.WhenAll inside a try and catch to collect failures, and a rollback path bolted on after something breaks halfway through.

You describe a process as a plain data record and a sequence of steps. EvalApp compiles that into one reusable execution path and gates every resource it touches (CPU, network, disk, database or a pool of your own) at a real bound. When you turn tuning on, it looks for the concurrency that works on the hardware it runs on, instead of a number someone picked once. It is the runtime under the other Evaluated Applications libraries, and it works on its own: no broker, no external service, no config store.

Why use it:
- One dependency instead of a stack. Where you would reach for a DI container, MediatR, Polly and TPL Dataflow, EvalApp is a single compiled pipeline that covers fan-out, resource gating, fallback steps and compensation together.
- The tuner probes, it does not wait for a failure. A circuit breaker waits for something to break and then responds. The adaptive tuner keeps probing for the operating point that stops things breaking, independently for each instance and with no coordination. A Bayesian mode keeps what it learned across restarts.
- Whole categories of coordination bugs do not compile. A saga you open has to be closed before the pipeline builds. A step with a side effect cannot be added without declaring the resource it touches, so there is no way to write an ungated side effect.
- The builder chain is the architecture. Read the fluent declaration from top to bottom and it reads like the process it describes. It is the code, not documentation about the code, so it cannot drift out of date the way a diagram does.
- Nothing to stand up first. It is a package reference, not infrastructure. Most pipeline libraries want a broker or a database before the first item is processed. EvalApp does not.

Capabilities:
- Fluent pipeline builder. Eval.App(...) leads to domains, tasks and steps, compiled once into an immutable, reusable ICompiledPipeline<T>.
- Resource-gated concurrency. Declare Network, DiskIO, Cpu, Database or a named pool of your own, and every step that touches it contends for the same bound.
- Adaptive and Bayesian tuning. A hill-climbing tuner that rediscovers the optimum on each run, or a Bayesian tuner whose performance model survives restarts. Both are opt-in and stay inside the bounds you declare.
- Parallel ForEach and parallel branches. Bounded per-item fan-out over a collection, where Tunable.ForItems() lets the tuner pick the count, and a fixed set of concurrent branches with configurable merge strategies.
- Sagas with compensation. Chain steps with an undo. When a later step fails, every earlier compensation runs in reverse order.
- Middleware. Wrap any step for retry, timing or audit by implementing IStepMiddleware<T>. It is a seam you implement, not a library of ready-made ones.
- Pipelines that run pipelines. A compiled pipeline is a value. A step can run another pipeline or itself, so an outer schedule loop can drive an inner per-batch pipeline, or a pipeline can recurse through a tree, with no orchestration code of your own. PipelineRef<T> forward-declares a pipeline, PipelineTrace tells same-named steps apart across levels, and runaway recursion fails cleanly instead of overflowing the stack.
- A harness for things that are not thread-safe. Declare an ExclusiveResource once (a GPU context, a native handle, a single-writer file), guard a scope or named branches with it, and a second concurrent entry fails loudly or queues, as you choose. It is re-entrant for recursion, and forks inside a held scope exclude each other.
- Single-thread hosts. In a browser, on a one-core process or when you say so, EvalApp detects it once and stops fanning out. ForEach, parallel groups and ChunkedWork run inline, and long runs hand the thread back every few milliseconds so a page stays responsive. On a multi-core host none of it is active.
- Results as data. PipelineResult<T> is Success, Failure or Skipped, matched with a switch instead of caught.
- Offline licence check. The licence validator every Evaluated Applications package embeds is part of the package. It runs entirely offline with ECDsa P-256 and makes no network call.

Quick start:

```csharp
using EvalApp;

Eval.App("Orders")
    .DefineDomain("Orders")
        .DefineTask<OrderData>("ProcessOrder")
            .AddStep("Validate", d =>
            {
                if (d.Total <= 0) throw new InvalidOperationException("Total must be positive");
                return d with { Status = "Validated" };
            })
            .AddStep("ApplyDiscount", d => d with { Total = d.Total * 0.9m })
            .AddStep("Complete", d => d with { Status = "Complete" })
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<OrderData> pipeline)
    .Build();

// Build once, at startup. Run as many times as you like.
var result = await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Alice", 99.99m));

switch (result)
{
    case PipelineResult<OrderData>.Success success:
        Console.WriteLine($"{success.Data.Status}: {success.Data.Total}");
        break;
    case PipelineResult<OrderData>.Failure failure:
        Console.WriteLine($"Failed: {failure.Exception.Message}");
        break;
    case PipelineResult<OrderData>.Skipped skipped:
        Console.WriteLine($"Skipped: {skipped.Reason}");
        break;
}

// Top-level statements come first, so the record goes last.
public sealed record OrderData(string CustomerName, decimal Total, string Status = "New");
```

Output:

```text
Complete: 89.991
```

Limits:
- Work that has to survive a process restart over hours or days belongs to a workflow engine such as Temporal. EvalApp runs in process.
- Purely reactive resilience, which detects a break and responds to it, is what Polly is for. EvalApp is for the case in between: no infrastructure to stand up, throughput that matters and concurrency that tunes itself.
- ICompiledPipeline<T> is opaque. It exposes a name and RunAsync. Report() gives a read-only view of the plan, with call counts for each ForEach node.
- The builder and step-construction path is safe to trim and to compile ahead of time. The tuner's file persistence and a couple of internal caches still use reflection-based JSON and raise trimmer warnings under PublishTrimmed, so leave WithTuning off if that matters for your build.
- The package ships as a binary with no source and no XML documentation. Author against the root EvalApp namespace; everything public lives there.

#### EvalApp docs (https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/evalapp/docs/)

A practical guide to building with EvalApp. Describe a process as a typed data record and a sequence of steps, gate every resource it touches, and let tuning find the concurrency that suits the hardware. Every program on this page is compiled and run against the published package.

##### Install

Add the package with dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.EvalApp. It targets net8.0 and net10.0 and has no dependencies, so the package reference is the whole installation.

The package ships as a binary, without source or XML documentation. Author against the EvalApp namespace and let IntelliSense on the public types be your reference.

The fluent builder and the AddStep<TStep>() and AddBranch<TStep>() step-construction paths are safe to trim and to compile ahead of time. The tuner's JSON file persistence and a couple of internal reflection caches are not fully trim-clean, so leave WithTuning off if you publish trimmed and that matters to you.

##### One namespace

Everything you need lives in the root EvalApp namespace: Eval, IAppBuilder, ResourceKind, Tunable, PipelineResult<T>, ICompiledPipeline<T>, the step base classes and licensing. The engine underneath lives in a separate EvalAppEngine namespace that is not part of the supported public surface. If something you need is not reachable from EvalApp, that is a gap to report, not a reason to reach into the engine.

##### Your first pipeline

The quick start on the overview page builds a three-step order pipeline. Four things in it carry through everything below.

- AddStep: Takes a name and a lambda, an async lambda, an IStep<T> instance or a PureStep<T> or AsyncStep<T> subclass.
- Records and with: Each step returns a new value. That is what makes a parallel ForEach safe without locks: no step can see another step's unfinished state.
- Run, then Build: Run(out pipeline) hands you the compiled, reusable pipeline, and Build finalizes the whole app. Build once at startup and call RunAsync many times. Rebuilding per request throws away everything the tuner has learned.
- Results as a union: PipelineResult<T> is Success, Failure or Skipped. Pattern-match it, or use GetData(), IsSuccess, IsFailure and IsSkipped when you only need the value.

##### Design before you build

The biggest lever on whether a pipeline reads cleanly is answering these questions before touching the builder. Each answer constrains the next.

- 1. What is the unit of work?: One sentence: one order, one invoice, one request, one batch.
- 2. What does it start with, carry and produce?: List every piece of information that exists at any point and encode it as a record. A non-nullable field is a required input, a nullable one is an output that appears once its step runs, and a bool is control (loop, branch, skip). If you cannot describe the whole lifecycle by reading the fields, the design is not finished.
- 3. What resource does each operation touch?: Classify each operation as Network, DiskIO, Cpu, Database, a custom ResourceKind.Of("name"), or none. This decides which operations need a gate.
- 4. What runs per item in parallel?: Independent items in a collection, which must not read each other's unfinished state, are ForEach boundaries.
- 5. What conditional branches exist?: For every If and Else, the condition, what each side does, and whether both write the same fields.
- 6. What must be rolled back on failure?: Walk the steps asking what has happened outside the process by the time each completes: money moved, mail sent, a record written. Only external effects need compensation.
- 7. Wire it together: Only now write the fluent declaration. If it does not read like a plain description of the process, the data model needs more work, not more code.

A single-item pipeline with no branches and no external effects skips straight to a flat sequence of steps. That means the problem was simple, not that the method failed.

##### Steps: pure, async and side-effecting

PureStep<T> is a synchronous transform with no side effects, and AsyncStep<T> is the same for work that waits on a network, a disk or a database. A step whose job is a side effect (a database write, a published event, an email) derives from SideEffectStep<T> and declares the ResourceKind it touches.

A SideEffectStep<T> cannot be added with the plain AddStep(name, instance) overload, which fails to compile. Add it with AddStep<TStep>(), which gates it on its declared resource, or with AddStep<TStep>(name, factory) when it needs a constructor-injected dependency. The resource has to be registered on the app first, with WithResource. If you would rather gate explicitly, write the side effect as an async lambda inside a Gate and the gate supplies the resource. Either way there is no path to an ungated side effect.

```csharp
using EvalApp;

Eval.App("StepKinds")
    .WithResource(ResourceKind.Network)   // a side-effect step is gated on its declared resource
    .DefineDomain("Orders")
        .DefineTask<OrderData>("ProcessOrder")
            .AddStep("Tax", new ApplyTaxStep())                  // PureStep<T> instance
            .AddStep("Fetch", new FetchTotalStep())              // AsyncStep<T> instance
            .AddStep<SendConfirmationStep>("SendConfirmation")   // SideEffectStep<T>: AddStep<TStep>() only
            .AddStep<PublishEventStep>("Publish", () => new PublishEventStep(new InMemoryBus()))
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<OrderData> pipeline)
    .Build();

var result = await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Alice", 100m));
var data = result.GetData();
Console.WriteLine($"{data.Status}: total {data.Total}, tax {data.Tax}");

public sealed record OrderData(string CustomerName, decimal Total, string Status = "New", decimal Tax = 0m);

public sealed class ApplyTaxStep : PureStep<OrderData>
{
    public override OrderData Execute(OrderData data) => data with { Tax = data.Total * 0.08m };
}

public sealed class FetchTotalStep : AsyncStep<OrderData>
{
    public override async ValueTask<OrderData> ExecuteAsync(OrderData data, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await Task.Yield();                       // real code: await the actual I/O here
        return data with { Total = data.Total + 1m };
    }
}

public sealed class SendConfirmationStep : SideEffectStep<OrderData>
{
    public override ResourceKind? ResourceKind => EvalApp.ResourceKind.Network;
    public override async ValueTask<OrderData> ExecuteAsync(OrderData data, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await Task.Yield();
        return data with { Status = "Confirmed" };
    }
}

public interface IOrderEventBus { ValueTask PublishAsync(string evt, CancellationToken ct); }
public sealed class InMemoryBus : IOrderEventBus
{
    public ValueTask PublishAsync(string evt, CancellationToken ct) => ValueTask.CompletedTask;
}

// A constructor-injected dependency: AddStep<TStep>(name, factory) builds it without a parameterless constructor.
public sealed class PublishEventStep(IOrderEventBus bus) : CrossDomainStep<OrderData, IOrderEventBus>(bus)
{
    public override ResourceKind? ResourceKind => EvalApp.ResourceKind.Network;
    public override async ValueTask<OrderData> ExecuteAsync(OrderData data, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await Shared.PublishAsync("OrderPlaced", ct);
        return data with { Status = "Published" };
    }
}
```

Output:

```text
Published: total 101, tax 8.00
```

##### Context-aware steps

When a step needs data that is constant for a whole app run (a configuration, a connection factory) or for a whole domain (a tenant, a region), subclass GlobalContext or DomainContext instead of threading it through every record. The context is populated on the step before it runs.

- Add with AddStep<TStep>(): ContextPureStep and ContextSideEffectStep do not implement the plain IStep<T> that the instance overload expects, so AddStep(name, instance) does not compile for them.
- No StepContext parameter: The public base classes never take one. A type of that name belongs to the internal engine and does not compile against the published package.
- Exceptions become results: Context steps catch their own exceptions and report a Failure, unlike the plain step kinds, which let the exception reach the pipeline.

```csharp
using EvalApp;

Eval.App("Context")
    .WithContext(new AppGlobal { Prefix = "ORD" })
    .DefineDomain("Orders", new OrderDomain { Region = "US" })
        .DefineTask<OrderData>("ProcessOrder")
            .AddStep<TagWithRegionStep>("TagRegion")   // context steps are added with AddStep<TStep>() only
            .AddStep<NotifyStep>("Notify")
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<OrderData> pipeline)
    .Build();

var result = await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Alice", 10m));
Console.WriteLine(result.GetData().Status);

public sealed record OrderData(string CustomerName, decimal Total, string Status = "New");
public sealed class AppGlobal : GlobalContext { public string Prefix { get; init; } = ""; }
public sealed class OrderDomain : DomainContext { public string Region { get; init; } = ""; }

public sealed class TagWithRegionStep : ContextPureStep<AppGlobal, OrderDomain, OrderData>
{
    protected override ValueTask<OrderData> TransformAsync(
        OrderData data, AppGlobal global, OrderDomain domain, CancellationToken ct)
        => ValueTask.FromResult(data with { Status = $"{global.Prefix}:{domain.Region}" });
}

public sealed class NotifyStep : ContextSideEffectStep<AppGlobal, OrderDomain, OrderData>
{
    protected override async ValueTask<OrderData> ExecuteAsync(
        OrderData data, AppGlobal global, OrderDomain domain, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await Task.Yield();   // real code: the actual notification I/O
        return data with { Status = data.Status + ":Notified" };
    }
}
```

Output:

```text
ORD:US:Notified
```

##### Gates and resource kinds

A Gate declares that everything inside it contends for a named, shared resource. The built-in kinds are Network, DiskIO, Cpu and Database, and ResourceKind.Of("name") defines a pool of your own. Declare a resource's bounds at the app level with WithResource, then gate any block of steps against it.

Without tuning, a gate holds at its declared default. With tuning on, the tuner moves it inside the declared minimum and maximum.

- Tunable.Between(min, max, default): Explicit bounds.
- Tunable.FixedAt(value): Minimum, maximum and default are the same, so there is nothing to tune.
- Tunable.ForCpu(): Scales with the number of processors.
- Tunable.ForItems(): A bound for per-item fan-out, which the tuner can move.
- Tunable.ModelOps(): Fixed at 1, for exclusive access such as GPU training.
- Tunable.DiskIo() and Tunable.Network(): Starting points for those two resource kinds.

```csharp
using EvalApp;

Eval.App("Gate")
    .WithResource(ResourceKind.Database, Tunable.Between(1, 8, 2))
    .WithResource(ResourceKind.Of("report-engine"), maxConcurrency: 1)
    .DefineDomain("Orders")
        .DefineTask<OrderData>("ProcessOrder")
            .Gate(ResourceKind.Database, onWaiting: null, configure: g => g
                .AddStep("CheckInventory", d => d with { Status = "Checked" }))
            .Gate("CustomPool", Tunable.FixedAt(1),
                onWaiting: null,
                configure: g => g.AddStep("RunReport", d => d with { Status = "Reported" }))
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<OrderData> pipeline)
    .Build();

var result = await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Alice", 10m));
Console.WriteLine(result.GetData().Status);

public sealed record OrderData(string CustomerName, decimal Total, string Status = "New");
```

Output:

```text
Reported
```

##### Parallel collections: ForEach

ForEach runs an independent pipeline over each item of a collection and merges the results back in source order. select extracts the collection, merge combines the results into the parent, and configure builds the per-item pipeline. Parallelism can be a plain number, a function re-read on each run, or a Tunable that the tuner can move.

A ForEach with fewer items than its minimum for parallel work runs inline on the calling thread, whatever the bound says, and the same is true when adaptive dispatch has learned that the items are cheap. The bound caps a fan-out; it never forces one. maxParallelism of 1 is always strictly sequential. Report() shows which path each ForEach took.

- CollectAndThrow: The default. Every item runs and, if any failed, the result is a Failure carrying every exception.
- FailFast: Remaining items are cancelled as soon as one fails.
- ContinueOnError: Failed items are dropped and the result is a Success with the survivors.

For a tight, pure-CPU loop over many cheap rows, repeated many times, use ChunkedWork instead. It fans out in chunks with scratch space allocated once per chunk, which is the right cost model when a per-item pipeline would dominate the work.

```csharp
using EvalApp;

var progress = 0;

Eval.App("ForEach")
    .DefineDomain("Orders")
        .DefineTask<LineItemsData>("CalcLineTotals")
            .ForEach(
                select: d => d.Items,
                merge: (d, items) => d with { Items = items.ToList() },
                collectionName: "Items",
                parallelism: Tunable.ForItems(),
                configure: sub => sub
                    .OnItemCompleted((item, result) => Interlocked.Increment(ref progress))
                    .AddStep("Calc", (LineItem i) => i with { LineTotal = i.Price * i.Quantity }))
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<LineItemsData> pipeline)
    .Build();

var items = Enumerable.Range(1, 12).Select(n => new LineItem($"item-{n}", n, 2.5m)).ToList();
var result = await pipeline.RunAsync(new LineItemsData(items));
var total = result.GetData().Items.Sum(i => i.LineTotal);
Console.WriteLine($"items: {result.GetData().Items.Count}, progress callbacks: {progress}, total: {total}");

public sealed record LineItem(string Name, int Quantity, decimal Price, decimal LineTotal = 0m);
public sealed record LineItemsData(List<LineItem> Items);
```

Output:

```text
items: 12, progress callbacks: 12, total: 195.0
```

##### Conditional and parallel branches

If takes a condition and builder actions for the then and else sides. Without an else and with a false condition the step reports Skipped. Classify is a first-match-wins cascade that names the pattern instead of repeating near-identical If blocks.

AddParallelGroup runs a fixed set of branches at once, as opposed to ForEach, which runs one pipeline per item. Branches that write different fields merge cleanly by default. When two branches might write the same field and that should be a conflict, pass an IMergeStrategy<T>.

```csharp
using EvalApp;

Eval.App("Branches")
    .DefineDomain("Orders")
        .DefineTask<OrderData>("ProcessOrder")
            .If(d => d.Total > 100,
                then: b => b.AddStep("VipDiscount", d => d with { Total = d.Total * 0.8m, Status = "VIP" }),
                @else: b => b.AddStep("StandardProcess", d => d with { Status = "Standard" }))
            .AddParallelGroup(
                pg => pg
                    .AddBranch("CalcTax", d => d with { Tax = d.Total * 0.08m })
                    .AddBranch<CalcShippingBranch>("CalcShipping")
                    .AddBranch("CalcHandling", new CalcHandlingFeeStep()),
                mergeStrategy: new SumNumericFieldsMerge())
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<OrderData> pipeline)
    .Build();

foreach (var total in new[] { 50m, 200m })
{
    var d = (await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Alice", total))).GetData();
    Console.WriteLine($"{d.Status}: total {d.Total}, tax {d.Tax}, shipping {d.Shipping}, handling {d.Handling}");
}

public sealed record OrderData(string CustomerName, decimal Total, string Status = "New",
    decimal Tax = 0m, decimal Shipping = 0m, decimal Handling = 0m);

public sealed class CalcShippingBranch : PureStep<OrderData>
{
    public override OrderData Execute(OrderData data) => data with { Shipping = 9.99m };
}

public sealed class CalcHandlingFeeStep : IStep<OrderData>
{
    public ValueTask<OrderData> ExecuteAsync(OrderData data, CancellationToken ct = default)
        => ValueTask.FromResult(data with { Handling = 1.5m });
}

public sealed class SumNumericFieldsMerge : IMergeStrategy<OrderData>
{
    public OrderData Merge(OrderData original, IReadOnlyList<OrderData> results)
        => original with
        {
            Tax      = results.Max(r => r.Tax),
            Shipping = results.Max(r => r.Shipping),
            Handling = results.Max(r => r.Handling),
        };
}
```

Output:

```text
Standard: total 50, tax 4.00, shipping 9.99, handling 1.5
VIP: total 160.0, tax 12.800, shipping 9.99, handling 1.5
```

##### Sagas: compensation on failure

A saga chains steps that each declare an undo. If a later step fails, every earlier compensation runs in reverse order. BeginSaga and EndSaga bracket the block, and the compiler refuses a pipeline whose saga is left open.

- BestEffort: The default. Every compensation runs even if one of them throws.
- AbortOnFirst: Stop compensating at the first compensation that fails.
- SwallowErrors: Run every compensation and swallow any exception from them.

```csharp
using EvalApp;

Eval.App("Saga")
    .WithResource(ResourceKind.Database, Tunable.FixedAt(2))
    .DefineDomain("Orders")
        .DefineTask<OrderData>("ProcessOrder")
            .BeginSaga(CompensationPolicy.BestEffort)
                .AddStepWithCompensation(
                    "ReserveInventory",
                    forward:    d => d with { Status = "Reserved" },
                    compensate: d => { Console.WriteLine("compensate: release the inventory"); return d with { Status = "Unreserved" }; })
                .AddGate(
                    ResourceKind.Database,
                    onWaiting: null,
                    configure: g => g.AddStep("WriteLedger", d => d with { Total = d.Total }),
                    compensate: new RevertLedgerStep())
                .AddStep(
                    "ChargePayment",
                    d => d.Total > 1_000_000m
                        ? throw new InvalidOperationException("Payment declined")
                        : d with { Status = "Charged" })
            .EndSaga()
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<OrderData> pipeline)
    .Build();

var ok = await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Ivy", 10m));
var failed = await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Jin", 2_000_000m));
Console.WriteLine($"ok: {ok.IsSuccess}, status {ok.GetData().Status}");
Console.WriteLine($"failed: {failed.IsFailure}, status after compensation {failed.GetData().Status}");

public sealed record OrderData(string CustomerName, decimal Total, string Status = "New");

public sealed class RevertLedgerStep : IStep<OrderData>
{
    public ValueTask<OrderData> ExecuteAsync(OrderData data, CancellationToken ct = default)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("compensate: revert the ledger entry");
        return ValueTask.FromResult(data with { Status = "LedgerReverted" });
    }
}
```

Output:

```text
compensate: revert the ledger entry
compensate: release the inventory
ok: True, status Charged
failed: True, status after compensation New
```

##### Middleware

IStepMiddleware<T> wraps each named step individually, for timing, retry, audit or per-step tracing. No middleware ships ready-made; it is a seam you implement. To wrap the steps of a ForEach item pipeline, register an IStepMiddleware for the item type on that sub-builder.

An exception thrown by a step comes back as a Failure. An exception thrown by middleware outside the call to next is thrown from RunAsync on a top-level pipeline, and is a Failure only when the pipeline is nested in another. A ForEach whose item pipeline is a single synchronous step normally runs as one fused loop, and attaching middleware turns that fast path off.

##### Dependency injection

AddStep<TStep>(name) and AddBranch<TStep>(name) resolve the step through an IStepFactory. The default creates it with a public parameterless constructor. ServiceProviderStepFactory asks your container first and falls back to that for anything not registered.

The compiler enforces the new() constraint whichever factory you register, so a type needs a literal parameterless constructor even if the container always supplies the real one. The factory path is for plain IStep<T> implementers. A side-effect step that needs a constructor-injected dependency uses AddStep<TStep>(name, factory) instead.

```csharp
using EvalApp;

// Any real IServiceProvider works; this minimal one keeps the sample dependency-free.
var services = new SimpleServiceProvider();
services.Register(typeof(ValidateOrderStep), new ValidateOrderStep("DI-resolved"));

Eval.App("Di")
    .WithStepFactory(new ServiceProviderStepFactory(services))
    .DefineDomain("Orders")
        .DefineTask<OrderData>("ProcessOrder")
            .AddStep<ValidateOrderStep>("Validate")     // resolved from the container, not Activator
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<OrderData> pipeline)
    .Build();

var result = await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Alice", 10m));
Console.WriteLine(result.GetData().Status);

public sealed record OrderData(string CustomerName, decimal Total, string Status = "New");

public sealed class ValidateOrderStep : IStep<OrderData>
{
    private readonly string _tag;
    // AddStep<TStep>() needs a literal parameterless constructor; the tagged one is what the container supplies.
    public ValidateOrderStep() : this("default") { }
    public ValidateOrderStep(string tag) => _tag = tag;
    public ValueTask<OrderData> ExecuteAsync(OrderData data, CancellationToken ct = default)
        => ValueTask.FromResult(data with { Status = _tag });
}

public sealed class SimpleServiceProvider : IServiceProvider
{
    private readonly Dictionary<Type, object> _services = new();
    public void Register(Type type, object instance) => _services[type] = instance;
    public object? GetService(Type serviceType) => _services.TryGetValue(serviceType, out var s) ? s : null;
}
```

Output:

```text
DI-resolved
```

##### Pipelines that run pipelines

A compiled pipeline is a value. A step can run another pipeline or itself, and a context can hold a registry of them, so an outer schedule loop drives an inner per-batch pipeline, or a pipeline recurses through a tree, without a hand-written loop around RunAsync. A loop of that kind is invisible to gates and to the tuner; this is how it becomes visible.

PipelineRef<T> forward-declares a pipeline before it is built, PipelineTrace tells same-named steps apart across levels, and a recursion that runs away fails cleanly with PipelineRecursionException instead of overflowing the stack.

##### Exclusive resources

Some things are not thread-safe: a GPU context, a native handle, a file with one writer. Declare an ExclusiveResource once and guard a scope, or named parallel branches, with Exclusive. A second concurrent entry fails loudly with ExclusiveViolationException, or queues if you choose that policy. The guard is re-entrant for recursion, and forks inside a held scope exclude each other instead of silently inheriting it.

##### One-thread hosts

Fanning out only pays when there is a second thread to fan out to. EvalApp detects a single-thread host once, at startup: a browser running Blazor WebAssembly, a process with one processor or one allowed CPU, or a host you declare with ExecutionHost.OverrideSingleThreaded or WithSingleThread. In that mode ForEach, parallel groups and ChunkedWork run inline on the caller, and long runs hand the thread back to the host every few milliseconds (ExecutionHost.YieldBudget) so a page or UI stays responsive. The cancellation token is checked at each yield.

A single very long synchronous step cannot be sliced. Split it into smaller steps or items. Inside a UI, use ChunkedWork.ForAsync and ChunkedWork.RunAsync, which work in time slices. On a multi-core host none of this is active and nothing is added to the fast path.

##### Licensing

No feature in EvalApp is gated behind a tier or a licence key. Every pipeline shape on this page runs at its full declared concurrency whether or not you pass a key, the tuner attaches whenever you call WithTuning, and Build(null) behaves exactly like Build(key).

The licence check exists so that every Evaluated Applications package validates a key the same way. LicenseValidator.ForEvalApp().Check(key) returns Unlicensed or Licensed and never throws, and CheckPeriodic(key, interval) is cheap enough for a hot loop. Verification is entirely offline, with ECDsa P-256, and makes no network call.

EvalApp is proprietary software under a commercial licence. Evaluation and non-commercial development are licensed without a key; commercial, production or revenue-generating use needs a separate licence.

##### Tuning and inspecting

Two opt-in modes. WithTuning is reactive: it rediscovers the operating point on each start, which suits a long-running, stable, single-instance service. WithBayesianTuning is predictive: a performance model persists across restarts, which suits frequent restarts and many instances. Both take an optional store path and share one phase machine, so switching between them does not reset what was learned.

The defaults come from a simulation harness and are what WithTuning uses out of the box. To override them, load your own JSON file with WithTunerSettings(path); the file is read when you call it, and a missing or invalid path throws at that point.

ICompiledPipeline<T> is opaque on purpose: a name and RunAsync. The read-only window on a plan is pipeline.Report(), which lists the plan's nodes and, for each ForEach, how many calls ran inline and how many fanned out. ExecutionHost.Yields counts the yields a process has taken.

```csharp
using EvalApp;

var store = Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), "evalapp-tuning-sample.json");

Eval.App("Tuned")
    .WithResource(ResourceKind.Network, Tunable.Between(1, 8, 2))
    .WithTuning(storePath: store)
    .DefineDomain("Orders")
        .DefineTask<Batch>("Fetch")
            .ForEach(
                select: b => b.Items,
                merge: (b, items) => b with { Items = items.ToList() },
                collectionName: "Items",
                configure: sub => sub
                    .Gate(ResourceKind.Network, onWaiting: null, configure: g => g
                        .AddStep("Download", async (int i, CancellationToken ct) => { await Task.Delay(5, ct); return i + 1; })))
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<Batch> pipeline)
    .Build();

for (var run = 0; run < 5; run++)
    await pipeline.RunAsync(new Batch(Enumerable.Range(0, 16).ToList()));

// A read-only window on the compiled plan: each ForEach node counts its calls (and, in Inline and FanOut, how they ran).
foreach (var node in pipeline.Report().Of("ForEach"))
    Console.WriteLine($"{node.Label}: {node.Calls} calls");

File.Delete(store);

public sealed record Batch(List<int> Items);
```

Output:

```text
Items: 5 calls
```

##### Anti-patterns to avoid

The tuner and the gates can only account for work they can see. Anything that happens outside the declared pipeline is invisible to both.

- Task.WhenAll in a step: Use a declared ForEach instead.
- A background Task kept on the record: It races the pipeline, ungated.
- Async work around RunAsync: Work before or after the call, outside the pipeline, is unthrottled and untuned.
- A shared collection written from a ForEach item: It is not thread-safe. Let each item own its result and collect results in merge.
- Mutating the record: Use with. Mutation breaks the guarantee that makes parallel ForEach safe without locks.
- State in step instance fields: Steps are reused by every concurrent run. Per-run state belongs on the record.
- Rebuilding the pipeline per request: It discards everything the tuner has learned. Build once, run many times.
- Blocking calls in a synchronous step: Use the async overload, and pass the cancellation token to every awaited call.
- A hand-written loop or recursion around RunAsync: The loop is invisible to gates and the tuner. Layer and recurse through context instead.
- Guarding a non-thread-safe singleton with a comment: Use an ExclusiveResource.

##### Extension seams

Beyond the fluent API and the step base classes, four extension points are public: GlobalContext and DomainContext (subclass them for WithContext and DefineDomain), IMergeStrategy<T> (custom conflict handling for AddParallelGroup) and IPressureResource (a soft, non-blocking budget signal for Pressure and WithPressure). Everything else is internal to the engine.

Licence: Commercial licence for commercial use. Evaluation and non-commercial use are permitted. Terms at https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/licence/

### HoloDb: an embeddable SQL database for .NET

A SQL database inside your app that answers dashboard queries in microseconds, with transactions, similarity search and tables bigger than memory.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/holodb/
- Package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb, release 5.1.2: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb`
- Package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Client, release 1.5.2: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Client`
- Package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Protocol, release 1.1.2: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Protocol`
- Builds on: EvalApp, Phasor
- Used by: Prose
- Tools: The Analyst, Prose

Ten million rows. Dashboard answers in microseconds.

Put a SQL database inside your app that rolls up a ledger in a blink, ranks rows by resemblance and keeps ACID transactions. Tables can be bigger than memory.

- 0.02 ms: to total 10,000,000 invoices by status. DuckDB took 41.63 ms
- More than 1,600 times: faster than DuckDB on that rollup, and more than 120 times faster on all five dashboard rollups
- 3.3 times: faster than DuckDB on a join of 10,000,000 invoices to 200,000 customers
- 16 of 16: queries that returned the same rows as SQLite and DuckDB. The ones where HoloDb is slower are listed too

HoloDb is an embeddable SQL database for .NET with ACID transactions, similarity search and maintained aggregates. It stores data as holograms in a single associative store: every value is encoded as a phase vector and a row's columns are bound into one hologram, so the same copy of the data can be retrieved three ways. Exact lookup by primary key is ordinary SQL. Similarity search by content is the NEAREST clause. Analytics read a maintained total instead of scanning.

Applications that need relational storage, similarity search and fast dashboard rollups normally reach for three systems, a row store, a vector index and a cube or a pile of scans, and pay to keep them consistent. HoloDb is one embeddable package: a transactional store, an in-SQL similarity search, and aggregates whose response time does not grow with the table.

Why use it:
- No separate vector index. NEAREST ranks rows by resemblance to a partial description, in SQL, over the rows the table already holds. A close number or date, or a near-identical string, ranks ahead of a far or unrelated one, and the score is readable as a column.
- Aggregates do not scan. An integer column's running total is itself one maintained vector, so whole-table COUNT, SUM, MIN and MAX and single-column GROUP BY read that value directly, flat as the table grows from a thousand rows to tens of millions.
- Real ACID, and past RAM. Write-ahead logging with an fsync on each durable commit, crash recovery bounded by live data and not by write history, reader and writer locking, and paged tables on an 8 KB buffer pool that let a table exceed memory.

Capabilities:
- A substantial SQL dialect. CREATE TABLE, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT with DISTINCT, COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX and AVG, a single INNER JOIN, WHERE with AND, OR, NOT, LIKE, IN, BETWEEN and IN (SELECT ...), GROUP BY and HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT, ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN, indexes, EXPLAIN, and explicit BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK.
- Parameterized queries. Every Execute has a ? placeholder overload with positional binding, correctly quoted and escaped, beside the raw SQL string form.
- Content similarity in SQL. NEAREST ranks by graded closeness for numbers, dates and text, with a score column on request. From 8,000 rows an approximate sublinear index ranks candidates, and below that or whenever the query has a WHERE the ranking is an exact scan.
- Constant-time exact aggregates. COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX and single-column GROUP BY over integer columns are exact, not approximate. Real-number aggregates use a fast SIMD scan.
- Durable and larger than memory. A snapshot plus a short log gives recovery that tracks live data. Paged tables spill cold pages to disk and keep the maintained aggregates accurate there.
- Fast scans. A WHERE is evaluated over raw column arrays in tight loops, GROUP BY over INT and TEXT columns uses dense codes, and an equi-join on TEXT keys is a columnar hash join.
- Metering. A per-query usage meter reports the rows and bytes actually processed, for billing or observability.
- Embedded or networked. Use it in process, or run it as a server with a matching typed client and a columnar wire protocol. The same managed code also runs in a browser tab.
